cards.front: any vs unknown in one line?
cards.meaning: any means “trust me, don’t check”; unknown means “prove it before you use it.” Both mean the value could be anything; the difference is discipline.

cards.front: What does any allow that unknown does not?
cards.meaning: any opts out of checking: method calls and property access are allowed, including chains that will fail at runtime. unknown still means “I don’t know”; you must narrow or assert before use.
cards.example: let a: any = 'hello'; a.nonExistentMethod(); a.foo.bar.baz; // compile ok

cards.front: Why is u.toUpperCase() an error when u is unknown?
cards.meaning: unknown forbids operations until you prove the type. After typeof u === 'string', toUpperCase is allowed. Use unknown at boundaries (JSON, catch, untyped APIs); treat any as a last resort.
cards.example: let u: unknown = 'hello'; u.toUpperCase(); // Error — if (typeof u === 'string') u.toUpperCase();

cards.front: Assign to any/unknown vs assign from them — table?
cards.meaning: Assign to either: almost anything (both are roughly top types). Assign from any to a precise type: allowed without checks. Assign from unknown to a precise type: error unless narrowed or asserted. Call methods: allowed on any, error on unknown until narrowed. Spreads unsafety: any yes (contagious), unknown no (forces proofs).

cards.front: Why is any contagious?
cards.meaning: Anything that touches any often becomes any too — return values, inferred locals — so one any can disable large regions of the program.
cards.example: function f(x: any) { return x.foo; } const y = f(1); y.bar; // still any — no error

cards.front: Can you assign unknown to string without a check?
cards.meaning: No. unknown does not assign freely to string, User, or other precise types. After typeof x === 'string', const s: string = x is ok.
cards.example: function g(x: unknown) { const s: string = x; } // Error

cards.front: How is any a bottom-ish escape as well as a top type?
cards.meaning: Both any and unknown can receive almost any value (top-ish). any is also assignable to most types without proof — unsound by design. unknown is not assignable to other types without narrowing or assertion, which is why unknown preserves safety and any does not.

cards.front: How does any sneak in with noImplicitAny off?
cards.meaning: With noImplicitAny off (or weak inference), untyped parameters become any. function add(a, b) { return a + b } types a and b as any.
cards.example:
// noImplicitAny: false
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

cards.front: How do you stop implicit any on parameters?
cards.meaning: Enable strict / noImplicitAny; annotate parameters or rely on contextual typing.

cards.front: How do untyped libraries introduce any?
cards.meaning: Modules without types default to any exports (depending on noImplicitAny / skipLibCheck / allowJs). Missing @types/… is a classic infection source. Fix: add types, write a minimal .d.ts, or wrap the API behind a typed facade that takes unknown and validates.

cards.front: What does JSON.parse typically return, and the safe pattern?
cards.meaning: any, historically / typically. Assign to unknown, then validate with a type predicate or Zod. Prefer validate over as User right after parse.
cards.example: const data: unknown = JSON.parse(s); if (isUser(data)) { /* data is User */ }

cards.front: Why not JSON.parse(s) as User?
cards.meaning: It compiles with no runtime proof. The notes prefer validate (predicate or UserSchema.parse) over a blind assertion immediately after parse.

cards.front: Which silence tricks leak any?
cards.meaning: as any and // @ts-ignore to silence errors. Other leaks: Object.keys / some DOM APIs returning wide types (less extreme than any, but similar “widen then cast” habits), generic defaults T = any, and loosely typed test mocks.

cards.front: How are Object.keys and some DOM APIs like any leaks?
cards.meaning: They return wide types — less extreme than any, but they encourage the same widen-then-cast habit. Treat them as a source of unsound shortcuts, not as unknown-safe APIs.

cards.front: Why is T = any a leak?
cards.meaning: A generic default written as T = any reintroduces contagious any whenever callers omit the type argument. Prefer T = unknown (as in Page<T = unknown>) when a default is needed.

cards.front: What is catch (err) under useUnknownInCatchVariables / strict-ish defaults?
cards.meaning: err is unknown. Thrown values can be anything — not only Error. any would allow err.message even when err is a string. unknown forces instanceof Error (or similar) before property access.
cards.example: catch (err) { if (err instanceof Error) console.error(err.message); else console.error(String(err)); }

cards.front: Why is catch the most “anything can show up” path?
cards.meaning: You can throw strings, objects, or Error. That is why unknown is the right discipline: prove structure (instanceof Error) or stringify, instead of assuming .message exists.

cards.front: Why is catch (e: any) a mistake?
cards.meaning: It is an old habit that opts catch back into contagious any. Prefer the unknown catch variable and narrow.

cards.front: Where should you use unknown?
cards.meaning: At boundaries: JSON, catch, external APIs, message ports. Boundary in: unknown → narrow/validate → typed domain. Boundary out: serialize known types; don’t trust round-trips without parsing.

cards.front: Can you pass unknown around without narrowing?
cards.meaning: Yes, as a passthrough until inspected — logValue(v: unknown) may console.log(v) because logging does not require structure. You cannot operate on it as structured data (v.foo) without checks.

cards.front: When do people still use any, honestly?
cards.meaning: Rare, conscious cases: migrating a huge JS file (temporary); truly unrepresentable interop (then wrap and shrink the blast radius); exhausted type-system edge cases (document why; prefer unknown + assert). Never as the default for “I’ll fix types later” in new Nest/React code.

cards.front: What is the preferred order instead of reaching for any?
cards.meaning: 1) unknown + narrowing, 2) generics, 3) proper typings, 4) any only with a comment and a ticket to remove it.

cards.front: const user = u as User after JSON.parse — safer than any?
cards.meaning: It compiles with no runtime proof. Assertions are sometimes needed, but they are not safer than any if you assert wrongly. Prefer predicates or Zod, then assertion only at a validated boundary.

cards.front: Object or {} vs unknown for unvalidated input?
cards.meaning: Prefer unknown for “yet unvalidated.” Object and {} have different assignability quirks and do not force the same narrowing discipline.

cards.front: Is turning off noImplicitAny a valid way to save time?
cards.meaning: No. It is a listed misconception. Silent any on parameters infects the function and anything that consumes its returns.

cards.front: What happens if one helper is typed with any?
cards.meaning: That any poisons an entire feature: return types and inferred locals stay any, so crashes have no compile signal. unknown would have forced proofs at the use sites.

cards.front: Why doesn’t a User type validate JSON.parse?
cards.meaning: Erasure: types do not exist at runtime and do not validate JSON. unknown forces the validation step (typeof / instanceof / predicates / zod) you actually need before a typed value.

cards.front: What do strict and noImplicitAny block?
cards.meaning: Silent any — untyped parameters and weak inference that would otherwise disable checking without you noticing.

cards.front: Are unknown and any the same because both mean “anything”?
cards.meaning: Same “could be anything,” opposite checking rules. any skips checking and infects dependents; unknown requires narrowing before use.

cards.front: List sneaky any sources and mitigations?
cards.meaning: Implicit any (enable strict/noImplicitAny); untyped libs (@types, .d.ts, unknown facade); JSON.parse (unknown + validate); as any / @ts-ignore; T = any defaults; loose mocks. Prefer unknown + narrowing over blind as.
